did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens with the image of the LORD as a shepherd: “The LORD is my shepherd.” This image expresses trust that the LORD cares for a person and provides for their needs, and therefore it says: “I shall not want.”
Did you know? This verse contains two images of rest and guidance: green pastures where the sheep lie down, and quiet waters to which the shepherd leads them.

Did you know? The shepherd’s role in this psalm is not only to provide food and rest, but also to restore the soul and guide it in “paths of righteousness.” The verse emphasizes that this guidance is given “for his name’s sake.”

Did you know? In the fourth verse, the language shifts from speaking about the LORD in the third person to addressing him directly: “for you are with me.” This change emphasizes a sense of closeness precisely in a time of danger.

Did you know? The “rod” and “staff” are the shepherd’s tools depicted in the psalm. In this verse, they symbolize guidance, support, and protection, and therefore they bring comfort even in the dark and threatening valley.

Did you know? In the fifth verse, the image changes: the picture of a shepherd and sheep gives way to the image of a host preparing a table. The table is set “in the presence of my enemies,” emphasizing the possibility of experiencing abundance and security even in the presence of enemies.

Did you know? The description of the head anointed with oil and the overflowing cup expresses generous hospitality and abundance. The phrase “my cup overflows” describes a cup filled to the point of satisfaction.

Did you know? The closing verse describes “goodness and mercy” as pursuing the speaker all the days of his life. It then expresses the hope of dwelling in the house of the LORD for length of days, bringing the psalm to a close with an enduring hope rather than merely momentary deliverance.
